---
title: "Readings — Fragmentation and size control"
---

Reading is optional but each item is here for a reason. Start with the two marked **start
here** if you read nothing else.

## Papers

**Rohland N, Reich D (2012).** *Cost-effective, high-throughput DNA sequencing libraries for
multiplexed target capture.* Genome Research 22:939–946.
[doi:10.1101/gr.128124.111](https://doi.org/10.1101/gr.128124.111) — **start here**

> A home-made bead clean-up written out in full, with the PEG and salt concentrations given.
> Read it to see that a "bead ratio" is a recipe you can write down and change, not a property
> of a brand.

**DeAngelis MM, Wang DG, Hawkins TL (1995).** *Solid-phase reversible immobilization for the
isolation of PCR products.* Nucleic Acids Research 23:4742–4743.
[doi:10.1093/nar/23.22.4742](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/23.22.4742)

> Two pages that introduce the carboxyl-bead, PEG and salt method that SPRI is named after. Look
> for how DNA is released again in low salt.

**Lis JT, Schleif R (1975).** *Size fractionation of double-stranded DNA by precipitation with
polyethylene glycol.* Nucleic Acids Research 2:383–390.
[doi:10.1093/nar/2.3.383](https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/2.3.383)

> The older, bead-free observation underneath it all: the PEG concentration needed to
> precipitate DNA depends on its length. Look at how the figures relate PEG and size.

**Adey A, Morrison HG, Asan, et al. (2010).** *Rapid, low-input, low-bias construction of
shotgun fragment libraries by high-density in vitro transposition.* Genome Biology 11:R119.
[doi:10.1186/gb-2010-11-12-r119](https://doi.org/10.1186/gb-2010-11-12-r119) — **start here**

> The paper that turned transposition into a fragmentation method. Look at how fragment size
> follows the enzyme-to-DNA ratio, and what the authors say about bias.

**Poptsova MS, Il'icheva IA, Nechipurenko DY, et al. (2014).** *Non-random DNA fragmentation in
next-generation sequencing.* Scientific Reports 4:4532.
[doi:10.1038/srep04532](https://doi.org/10.1038/srep04532)

> Evidence that "random" fragmentation methods are not quite random. Useful when a coverage
> dip or peak seems to follow the sequence.

**Boyle AP, Davis S, Shulha HP, et al. (2008).** *High-resolution mapping and characterization
of open chromatin across the genome.* Cell 132:311–322.
[doi:10.1016/j.cell.2007.12.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2007.12.014)

> A DNase I digest in human cells whose cut ends are the data. Look at how the digestion is
> limited and how tags are captured.

**Gillet NA, Malani N, Melamed A, et al. (2011).** *The host genomic environment of the
provirus determines the abundance of HTLV-1–infected T-cell clones.* Blood 117:3113–3122.
[doi:10.1182/blood-2010-10-312926](https://doi.org/10.1182/blood-2010-10-312926)

> Shows shear-point lengths used as a count of cells carrying an integration. Compare with the
> statistical treatment in Berry et al. 2012,
> [doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/bts004](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bts004).

**Velculescu VE, Zhang L, Vogelstein B, Kinzler KW (1995).** *Serial analysis of gene
expression.* Science 270:484–487.
[doi:10.1126/science.270.5235.484](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.270.5235.484)

> The classic fixed-length tag from a Type IIS enzyme. The method is obsolete, the idea is not:
> see where the tag is cut relative to the recognition site.

## Reference material to keep open

- [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts):
  recognition sequence, end type, and for Type IIS and IIG enzymes the cut offset
- Your bead supplier's size-selection application note, for the ratio-to-size table. Treat it
  as a starting point and calibrate on a ladder
- [NGS 101](https://henriksson-lab.github.io/NGS_101/): the protocol collection that this
  course draws its examples from
